newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP holding off on CSO decision.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP holding off on CSO decision.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd is undecided on whether it will sell diamonds from a new mine it hopes to develop in Canada's Northwest Territories through the De Beers CBR-controlled Central Selling Organisation (CSO), a BHP official told Reuters.
"We haven't decided how we are going to market them yet at all," William Zimmerman, BHP's marketing manager for diamonds, told Reuters in an interview.
BHP has so far spent around C$170 million on the Lac de Gras project, which is expected to yield on average 4.5 million carats a year for 25 years, Zimmerman said.
Depending on how negotiations go with local aboriginal groups over lands rights issues and environmental permits, the mine could be in operation by late 1998, he said.

Argyle Diamond Mines Pty Ltd of Australia earlier this year dropped out of the CSO, marking the first time since the 1970s that a diamond company sought independence from the London-based cooperative which is estimated to control about half the world's sales of rough diamonds.
Zimmerman said BHP was monitoring Argyle's move, but was in no rush to cement its own sales plan.
"We're leaving our options open at this time," he said.
Zimmerman said that with so many changes going on in the diamond industry there was no need to rush a decision.
He said it was likely BHP would hold off on a decision on whether to join the CSO until a year to 18 months before mine production started.
BHP has a 51 percent stake in the project. Dia Met Minerals Ltd holds 29 percent and the geologists who discovered the deposit and are major shareholders of Dia Met own the rest.
The Lac de Gras mine is BHP's first big step into diamonds.
Argyle is 60 percent-owned by RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd and 40 percent by Ashton Mining Ltd.
BHP is also is looking for diamonds in Guyana, southern Africa, Australia and elsewhere in Canada, but none of these projects is advanced, Zimmerman said.

The core of the Lac de Gras mine is being designed on five kimberlite ore pipes, or veins, three of which contain diamonds valued in the range of US$122.00-$130.00 a carat, placing them among the best in the world, he said.
Zimmerman said that while BHP was better known as producer of less glamorous commodities such as steel and copper, diamonds fitted the company's ideas for growth.
"Diamonds fit into the equation at the moment because we feel that we have to expand our product inventory and get into new industries in order to create the kind of growth that we want," he said.
"We just can't continue to expand coal and iron ore and copper to the degree that's going to give us the growth that we need," he said.
Government approval to proceed with development of the mine hinges on progress being made in negotiations between BHP and aboriginal groups on compensation agreements.
"We're hoping that will happen by October," Zimmerman said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
